videos.title: lars wahlgren   talent development in sweden (1080p)

segments.description: Coaches, please welcome Lars Borgern, a former World number 66 singles player and Australian indoor championship finalist. After a successful professional career, Lars transitioned to coaching becoming an accredited master professional with PTCA. In his session, talent development in Sweden Lars will share his insights and from his experiences mentoring players and fostering growth in the Swedish tennis system. Welcome. It's wonderful to see Lars here today. Lars, you've been such an outstanding player, 66 in the world. You burst onto the scene in Australia as a teenager against Lendl in the Australian indoor final way back in the 80s. You've been an accomplished coach, Fed Cup coach in Sweden. So many things about you. Just ooze class. Lars, welcome. Can you regale us a little bit about your match against Lendl back in the late 80s? It's so fantastic to be here today and talk about the good old memories. Of course, I had a good run before the Sydney Indoor in Australia. I was up in Queensland playing a satellite up at Rockhampton where the snakes were on the court. I was coming down to Brisbane to the Cubs record center. I was also playing a challenger before that and then coming into the Milton tennis center in Brisbane for the 80s. So I played probably like at that time, maybe eight weeks before that up in Queensland, four weeks in the satellite and a challenger and also Brisbane. Then coming down to Sydney,

I was well prepared, but I didn't have any expectations. I was ranked around 200, but I was feeling very welcomed in Australia. I was playing a lot in Australia. I was living in Australia as a Swede and then coming into the Sydney Indoor, playing qualifying and then playing the big guys, Charlie Steeve from Germany in the second round. He was 11 in the world and then in the quarter final, a bit slobbered on Sivoyanovic who won the final Wimbledon the year before. So I was underdog all the time and then at the fun time was at the Indoor semifinal. I played Johan Anderson living in Sydney. Yes, Australian. I was living back at his house and it was a fantastic moment. The whole week I was living with them, with the Swedish family, but he was playing for Australia and I beat him in the semis, which was an awkward time to live in the same house as Johan and his family, beating him in the semis and then going up against number one in the world and Ivan in the five sets, so it was fun. And of course he was at the peak of his powers then and that must have been an incredible experience and the camaraderie you had with other Swedes was immense at that time. You could probably be, you know, I think what you said was 66 in the world at some point, but you may not have even been in the Swedish top 10. It was a fun time for me, but I was always feeling as you say, I was around number 10 in the world when I was 66. We had Ed Berger's number one, Vilandar's number

two. We had the five in the top 10 at that time. Anders Jeroen, Joakim Nyström, Michael Pernfoss was 10. And these guys, I'm working a little bit now with the Swedish Federation as well, and the Swedish here in Sweden, so it's fun to see them again. But at that time we were traveling together and training hard. And when the Australian Open up came up, I think four months later, 1990, then we were 18 Swedes in the main draw for the Aussie Open. Wow, that's just incredible times, isn't it? Yeah. And I mean, just as we get on to that, you know, we're going to get dive into your coaching career in a moment, but Swedish tennis has changed a lot from those healthy and days of the 80s and 90s. What has made it change and where are you now? It is. It was some tough times. And I think at that time, Swedes, we came with something new. We had Björn Borg as the train, the local train, who showed us the way to win some matches. So everyone wanted to play like Björn, wanted to be like Björn. And after that, I think some people, they took us for granted and they just came up. Thomas Enquist, Magnus Larsson, they came up winning, winning, winning. Juniors come back and we were winning all the junior tournaments around the world as well. And then suddenly all the countries, I remember Spain came to Bosta to our tennis center and they came and they looked how we were doing. And they came back to Spain and then they put on maybe 20 more tournaments as well,

much more than what we had. They had big, a little bit more money and organization. And also now, I think it's tough with the four Grand Slams and Australia is one of them for us to compete with the money coming into the federations with all this... Indeed. ...French, France and also England, competing with all the possibilities they can bring with all the funding. Yeah. Yeah, no, that's well surmised. We're going to go into your coaching career now, Lars. You served as the Fed Cup captain from 2013 to 2016. You've coached a plethora of players from... or worked with a plethora of players from Steffi Graf to Nicholas Keefer. And I could just read out the list, but it's just exorbitant. What has been some of your finest coaching moments? I think it's always when you work, when you sit there on the side, you had done the preparations before the match. You have the... studying the opponent, so you have some tactic coming. When you see... at that moment, when you see your player following the tactic that you have been given and try and also, of course, winning at that with that moment, but you're very happy that you establish a good communication with the player. They understand you, they respect you and which is very important. And at that moment, you sit on the side, you have a tactic, they put it together and they start winning the... the winning matches because of that. It's a fantastic feeling.

And also, of course, when you end up on the Sunday with the trophy a few times, that doesn't happen every time, but when you do that, then it's a great moment. And luckily, I had this moment almost with every player. They were winning either smaller tournaments or a little bit bigger tournaments, but sometime of this coaching relationship, I had with our players, they won something. And that's a great feeling, I think, for the tournament. Yeah. And I think you've been a very diverse coach because you've worked a lot with female players as well and male players and that's a real credit to you. So, yeah. We're going to switch gears a little bit now into what you're doing in Sweden because you're doing some really interesting stuff with regional Swedish juniors. Tell us a little bit about that. Yeah, I mean, the last two years, I've been hired back into the Federation. I had like five years where I was freelancing a little bit and working as a myself coach, but with private things. But now I'm back with the Federation in the south and I'm doing a lot of different programs for between 10 and 15-year-old girls and boys in my regent. And my regent is quite big. It's like probably five-hour drive from top to bottom. So, it's a pretty big regent. We have 130 clubs, we have 35 members and I'm taking care of that together with two other guys and we have a good junior program, I think. And what I'm doing is because we have quite big differences from one

city to another. That's why I'm trying to get them together on the Saturday Sundays, not every Saturday, not every weekend, but we have weekend camps where they play eight-hour tennis, they do a little gym work, they live together, they train together, we play singles and doubles, and so that's what I'm doing. We feel in the Federation that these camps are important, that they play matches against each other because in the home environment, in the club, they do a lot of good work, they do a lot of practice with the coaches, with their own girls and boys around them. But that's why we try to take, for me, it's around 12 players, the optimal. We have 16-door courts right now, we play indoor from now onwards. We have 16-door courts, we have 12 players coming in from different clubs, the top, top 12 in every age group, and I collect them. The first hour we have, we have four in a court and we hit a lot of crosscourt and down the line and do a lot of warming up together. And then the other hour we have six courts and we play single matches and do that for the rest of the day and also the next day. And then in the last hour, we're back to three courts, we put them all together in doubles, so we're working single matches and doubles matches in two days, eight hour tennis, sort of, collect them. And in Stockholm, if we compare to Stockholm, then we have a little bit different because they have a possibility

that to work with them every week because Stockholm clubs, they're close to each other, and it's a different story. For us, we have far drive to different clubs, and in Stockholm, they have a possibility within one hour drive for all of the clubs, so they can, they're working a little bit different. But Stockholm and South, we are the dominating regent in Sweden right now. Yeah, no, that's really interesting because obviously Australia is such a big country and we certainly face those sort of challenges here regionally. And the, you know, the initiatives obviously you've got going in regional tennis, it's really important. Tell us, like, what are some of the challenges these kids in the regional areas have to sort of overcome? Like, obviously there's challenge, but, you know, just being able to play against, you know, they don't want to necessarily play against themselves all the time, bringing them in to play against the other city kids, that's obviously, you know, something you do. It is the challenge, I mean, we try to get them together, we try to just to bring them together as much as we can. But of course, they have the school, they have the school, they have the club, they have the team tennis matches, and it's a lot of things to take care of. And yeah, you have to really see what schedule fits them and so on. It's, it is, the school in Sweden is pretty tough and this kids we are talking about, they are in the

sixth grade, seventh grade, eighth grade, and it's a little bit different and it's tough for them, but they handle it well, and I'm working on the weekends for them, but it's not easy for them. It's a lot of tennis, a lot of traveling, and also then from my days when I played, we played between the ITF Tour and then the ATP of the WTA Tour. Now we have this tennis Europe Tour as well, under 12, under 14, under 16, which is a little bit of a professional tour, but it's a lot of competition and they're trying, they're traveling a lot in a very young age, which I don't know, it's, I don't think it's necessary in that age to travel so much, but some kids do that too. No, that's really interesting. You know, I guess you work a lot with their private coaches as well. Yes, we are, when I have the 10-year-old for example, we have this three hour get-together with collecting like seven clubs with seven coaches, one coach from every club, they have to bring four kids with them, a 10-year-old, and they all, you know, we have seven courts or six courts and we all play together, we put every 10-year-old on each court so they get to know new players, new coaches, and we all work together. Coaches start to mingle and talk about different possibilities, and so that's one of my key things is to get the coach, and then after my three hour tennis with these 20 kids, with five, six coaches, then for them, I want them

to start doing it themselves also, so it's not only under my umbrella, I say I'll take an initiative for the next month, they say put the hands up and say okay, next month we can do it in our club, we bring them all together again, they can practice, leave it, they can play some points, and maybe leave a little bit of food as well together, so that's why I think it's, we have to work together, we're a small country and we have to do it together. Yeah, and something that we've become cognizant here in Australia is this power of friendships and team tennis, which I think has eroded a little bit in the last 20 years, and you know that's very powerful if you can get them to become friends because obviously in your time coming up, you know, there were these stories of the lander sleeping in a caravan after he'd won the French Open with all his teammates and this sort of stuff, so you know developing that, that those these tight friendships. Yeah, I think as I know, I know the Australian way and also the Swedish way, going back these years with a very successful, we have two or three teams from Australia, remember the Woodies had one team to get me from me and then this sort of in the Federation team, we also have, Barry Moore was traveling with Russell Barlow and a few others, they had a few teams, we also had teams with Jonter Sjörgen as a head coach and together with Rilando Järvid

and Nyström was in one team and then we had another team with Enquist, Larsson and Kulti and that was very successful, these teams and nowadays I think it's more individual races and I think it's very expensive races and it's a lot of mostly now with these races and you have to have money to do this and I think in Sweden and Australia we were very strong around the world when we were working together with like three or four players together with one coach traveling with them and that's necessary, that's one thing we don't really do so much now in Sweden, we don't have coaches with them traveling as team and I think that's lacking the result of that. Yeah, no that's right, you really raised some really interesting sociological concepts there. What sort of virtues do you try to install into your players? Because anyone that saw you play, you were the hardest worker, you were incredibly, you had a massive heart on the court and you were never late for any practice session, you were incredibly articulate with what you did and how you planned, what are some of the virtues that you install in your players now? I think one thing is you have to do it simple, the thing that you can do ahead of a match or practice that you can really, really do is preparing, the preparing that you can be in charge of is very important, the racket string, the grip, the close, the shoes, all that you can sort of prepare before a match, do it and do it well, play with the same ball if

you can, now I'm talking about the professional way, but if you can, do it as much as the match is coming up and in the juniors, I think a lot of juniors, they're starting with parents, they're starting in the wrong end and I'm saying, I'm also a private coach, but I think that they're doing it in a different way that they're coming to the coaches, spending a lot of money and that's why I'm every weekend, I'm talking to parents around 10 and 11-year-old kids and I'm saying, please, you're spending a lot of money on hotels, you're spending a lot of money on coaches and one of the most important things is that to get the girl or boy, the fitness well first, the running, so when they're ready to do the lesson, you have to be able to also be able to run and be having energy for the whole lesson, not coming unfit and just do the tennis because you pay money and you think you're going to have good results because you're having a good coach, that's not the key, the key to prepare, the forest is free, I always say to all my players, they love me a lot, the forest is free, go out there for two weeks, come back, you have been running every day, then you're going to see the result on the court, the defeat and the legs are most important in tennis and if you don't like to run, I don't know if you're going to be a tennis player because you have to run to be a good tennis player. Yeah, no, that's absolutely

sage advice and I think a lot of people should listen to that, that virtue right there. And also one, another key I think is the spontaneous playing tennis. When you call me up in Melbourne, you call me up, you and I, we go out and play, we just don't have to have two coaches standing there with a basket of balls, you and I, we have four balls, we go out and play because we love it and I think that's the missing, one of the biggest keys in Sweden right now is that all the kids, they don't have the spontaneous, they don't cycle down with two rackets and play each other and just practice and play, very few kids does that. Most of them, they have to be organized, always with a coach, always in a group and then between five and six every Monday and Friday instead of when they're free of school, Saturday, Sunday, cycle down and play themselves. I think the spontaneous tennis and want to play tennis and love it, that's the key, that's the big... It's very, yeah, it's very engineered, isn't it now, unfortunately. How do you deal with that in Sweden? What are some things that are you doing with the kids now? No, I'm just trying to tell them that you don't have to have me on the court or another coach on the court all the time, just call your friend, call your friend, come down here and play and just, you know, a lot of them in the clubs in Boston, the kids, they can play for free there, so they, you have to, you can, I mean, the club can also help them to,

if you're under certain age, just come down here and the course of free, you can go on court, they don't have to be so organized, you just come out and play, there is the basket of balls, it's very easy, yes, and we're trying to do it, but I'm not working in a club, I work for the Federation a little bit, but there's one of the key things is that in the club, I'm the sort of together with a little bit in the same, same city, that's why I think they are doing a lot for the kids for the spontaneous, and that's, for example, it's free courts for them, they can come whenever they want and play. Yeah, no, that's wonderful, that's really given us a bit of a snapshot, if you like, of Swedish tennis. At the pointy end, is college an option now for Swedish kids as well? We are talking a lot about it now, we sort of having a lot of players that go to college, and we are sort of missing them as well, because I think our top players, we don't have so many right now, but the top players, they also need a good group around them, and a lot of the group, the second group of Swedish tennis, they're going off to college, which is a great idea, but we also need them back in Sweden to back up our top players to play the tournaments, but yes, it's a big producing of college players from Sweden. It's always been, I think, for me, we haven't seen many coming back with good results after four years in USA,

we have pernforce, but this is like, you know, 30 years ago, and then some of them, in my point of view, if you can have the time in your mind that you know that you are 18, and you're not fully developed, and you go over to USA for four years, and you have the just time and energy to be there for four years, do the education, and do the practice full-on, play your team, play your school matches, and then coming back after four years and be a very, very good player because the fundings and the possibilities in USA is fantastic, but you have to wait four years to be a professional player, and you have to really, really be patient, and I don't know if you have the energy and the patience to wait so long to be a professional, but the idea I think is great. Yeah, yeah, that's a good contention, and of course you've done really 360 in your career because you worked a lot with pros at the beginning of your coaching journey, and now you're working with the youth, so have you experienced that? I think it's fantastic, and I mean, I'm coaching also a little bit of adults and sometimes an adult, and soon they need to have the passion for tennis. If they have the passion for tennis, I think it's fantastic, and they say, oh, you have been coaching Steffi Graff, you have been coaching Adelaide Petrova, they have been winning Grand Slams, and now you're standing here with me, I said, yeah, but you are interested to learn, you listen, and nothing that's fantastic. As a coach,

all you want from your player, it's a junior, or adult, and a beginner, or a professional, when they have the respect and they listen to you, I think it's fantastic as a coach. What I come with me from the tennis, when I was coaching professional guys and professional girls, one thing that I try to mix and getting a good balance of, when I'm most coaching the girls, I find that the practice always, and don't always, but very often, they want to have a lot of rhythm, they want to play the cross court, they want to know where the ball was coming, they want to practice, they want to have a good feeling every time, every practice was the same, with a lot of cross court down the line, and models, with coaching the boys, the professional guys, they wanted to play points a lot, always points, oh, we want to play points, we hit five minutes, then we want to play points, doesn't matter where we were, always wanted to play points. If you can find something in the middle, I think it's very important as a coach, if you can find a player, guy who wants to play points, but if you can also find that they need the rhythm tennis as well, the cross court, and they need a few like balance of that, and then the girls, they also need to learn to not only play with the coach, they also need to learn to play points. If you can take a little bit from the boys over to the girls, and leave it from the girls over to the boys, I think

they have the perfect practice. The perfect mix. Once again, they're amazing pearls of wisdom, and I think it says a lot about you, your humble disposition of what you just said about the adults, and being at the very pointy end of the coaching and then journey, and then your coaching adults at a local club, I think that's just amazing humility, and it just speaks a lot about what you are, and people, there'll be a lot of people here in Australia that will remember you, and of course this is going around the world, so I think it's a great place now to stop, and thanks for being part of this last. Oh thank you so much, and I always, when I came to Australia first time, I always felt very, very welcome as a player, and when I was in Queensland, or Sydney, or Perth, or Adelaide, or very much in Melbourne as well, they were always great players, great friends, I played the MCG for the pennant, the team tennis there, I played a lot of satellites in Dendipark and Dingley, and also in Queensland and around Australia, and one of my great memories was when I was playing Hoffman Cup for Sweden, but also coaching, now the Petrova to win the Hoffman Cup in Perth, so unbelievable memories from Australia, and the people there has been so welcome for the Swedes, I think all the Swedish players, I can talk to Jonas Björkman, Stefan Edberg, Magnus Gustafsson, they all say the same, we land there, they all say that they love Australia,

and we have always been feeling there, as a Swede, always feeling very, very welcome as a player, and as a tourist, so it's fantastic. Yeah, no indeed, and that's definitely the memories I have of you as well. Thanks a lot. Thank you very much.
